title: Hudhayfah, keeper of secrets
hook: the keeper of secrets, who asked about harm so he could avoid it

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Musa, whose recitation the Prophet heard in the night. Your line was a voice like Dawud's.

What brings reward? What is best? Those were the questions people brought to the Prophet. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, a companion, later tells his listeners how his own questions ran the other way. People used to ask the Messenger of God about the good, he says. I used to ask him about the evil, because I was afraid it would catch me. Plenty of us collect advice about what to do. Hudhayfah collected warnings. Today: Hudhayfah.
screen: `THEY ASKED ABOUT THE GOOD.` → `HE ASKED ABOUT THE EVIL.` → `AFRAID IT WOULD CATCH HIM.`

segments.voice: That sentence opens a long report in Sahih al-Bukhari. Hudhayfah asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: we were in ignorance and harm, and God brought us this good. Will there be harm after this good? Yes, the Prophet says. And after that harm, good again? Yes, but with some smoke in it, some haze. Hudhayfah keeps pressing for the next turn and the next, until he asks the practical one: if that time reaches me, what do you command me to do? The point of all the asking was not gloom. It was a plan: find out where the road gets dangerous so you can walk around it. His fellow companions noticed something else. In Bukhari, Abu al-Darda refers to Hudhayfah as the one among them who holds the secret that no one else knows. Tradition says the Prophet had told him things he told no one else, including who among the people of Medina were hypocrites, and that Hudhayfah kept it. Some reports say even Umar would ask him, worried, whether his own name was on that list, and that Hudhayfah would only say no to him, and name no one else. Those details come from later reports, not from Bukhari. So the man who asked about harm was also trusted with hard knowledge, and he didn't spend it on gossip. Knowing where the danger was did not make him suspicious of everyone. It made him careful with himself, and quiet about others.
screen: `WILL THERE BE HARM AFTER THIS?` · `GOOD AGAIN, BUT WITH HAZE.` · `WHAT DO YOU COMMAND ME TO DO?` · `THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE SECRET.` · then, large: `ASK ABOUT THE HARM.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself Hudhayfah's question, pointed inward: where does harm usually catch me? A certain hour of the night, a certain app, a conversation that always turns sour, anger when I'm hungry. Don't scold yourself; just name it, the way you'd mark a pothole on your street, and if you pray, ask for protection from it.
Hudhayfah. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, the companion who asked the Prophet about harm so he could avoid it, remembered as the keeper of secrets. Today's word.
Your line: ask about the harm. A warning heard early becomes a plan. Eight hundred sixty days, and counting.

screen: `DAY 860 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SALIM, MU'ADH AND THE OTHERS.`

howItsDone: Muslims quote Hudhayfah's words about asking of evil in order to avoid it, and scholars cite his long report in Bukhari when discussing how to hold fast during times of trouble.
